Honest answers
The questions every tools site should answer straight. Are the tools really free?
Yes — every tool on this page is free to use, with no account, no trial and no locked features. If that ever changes, it will be written here in plain words, not hidden. Do my files get uploaded to a server?
No. The image compressor, password generator, QR maker and every other tool run with JavaScript inside your own browser. Close the tab and nothing remains — there is no server collecting your files. Where do the thumbnails come from?
Directly from YouTube’s public image servers, the same files YouTube itself shows. If a creator never uploaded a custom thumbnail, some sizes simply don’t exist — the tool tells you instead of faking a result. Is the YouTube money calculator accurate?
It is an estimate, and it says so. Real earnings vary with niche, viewer country, season and advertiser demand. Use the range for planning, and trust YouTube Studio’s revenue tab for your real numbers. Who runs this site?
The creator of Empire of Money and Qabristan Ki Awaz — two YouTube channels about the history of money and animated horror stories. The tools came first from our own everyday workflow as creators. Why do some tools look different from big sites?
Because this page was written from scratch for this site. Every tool here is original code built for TOOLZORQ — tested one by one before being listed. Guides

# How to Check Your YouTube Title and Description Before You Publish — https://basr.me/guides/youtube-title-description-checker-guide.html

YouTube cuts off titles and descriptions that run too long, and it counts every character — including spaces. Checking your text against YouTube's actual limits before you hit publish takes a minute and saves you from a title that ends mid-sentence. This guide shows how to do it with TOOLZORQ's free Title & Description Checker.

## Know the limits first

YouTube's limits are:

- Title: 100 characters
- Description: 5,000 characters
- Tags: 500 characters in total

Staying inside these limits is only part of the job — the first words of your title and description are also what viewers actually see in search results and on their home feed, so put the most important words first.

## Use TOOLZORQ's Title & Description Checker

The Title & Description Checker is one of the free tools on TOOLZORQ's homepage. It runs entirely in your browser, with no sign-up and nothing to install. To use it:

1. Open TOOLZORQ and find the Title & Description Checker among the tools.
2. Type or paste your video title into the title box — the character count updates live against the 100-character limit.
3. Do the same for your description (limit 5,000 characters) and your tags, separated by commas (500 characters in total).
4. Trim anything that runs over the limit before you copy the text into YouTube Studio.

Because the counts update as you type, you can try a shorter wording on the spot and see immediately whether it fits.

## Write for the cut-off, not just the limit

A title can be within the 100-character limit and still get cut off in search results, where viewers only see the beginning. The same goes for descriptions, where only the first couple of lines show before a viewer has to tap "more". Practical habits that help:

- Front-load the title: put the topic and the hook in the first few words, not at the end.
- Lead the description with the summary: the first one or two sentences should say what the video is about, so a viewer who never expands the description still gets the point.
- Keep tags focused: a short list of relevant tags beats a long list of loosely related ones, and it is easier to stay inside the 500-character total.

Rule of thumb: if your title only makes sense when read in full, rewrite it so the first half already tells the story. Then check the full version against the limit.

## Quick checklist

- Is the title within 100 characters?
- Does the beginning of the title make sense on its own?
- Is the description within 5,000 characters, with the summary up front?
- Are the tags comma-separated and within 500 characters in total?
- Did you paste the checked text into YouTube Studio, rather than retyping it from memory?

# How to Compress Images for Faster Uploads Without Losing Quality — https://basr.me/guides/compress-images-for-faster-uploads.html

Large photos are the most common reason an upload stalls or a page loads slowly. A phone photo can easily be several megabytes, while the version a website, form, or chat app actually needs is often a fraction of that size. Compressing the image first — shrinking the file without visibly changing the picture — makes uploads faster and avoids rejected attachments. This guide shows how to do it with TOOLZORQ's free Image Compressor.

## What compression actually does

An image file stores colour and detail information for every pixel. Compression reduces that file in two ways: by resizing the picture to smaller dimensions, and by saving it in a format that stores the same visible picture more efficiently. A photo shown at 1200 pixels wide does not need to be stored at 4000 pixels wide — the extra pixels are invisible to the viewer but still take up space and upload time.

The goal is not the smallest file possible. Push compression too far and text goes fuzzy, faces lose detail, and flat colours develop visible banding. The sweet spot is the smallest file that still looks the same as the original at the size it will actually be viewed.

## Use TOOLZORQ's Image Compressor

The Image Compressor is one of the free tools on TOOLZORQ's homepage. It runs 100% in your browser using the canvas engine — your photo is never uploaded anywhere, so it is safe for personal photos and screenshots. It accepts JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF (first frame) and more. To use it:

1. Open TOOLZORQ and find the Image Compressor among the tools.
2. Drop your image into the tool, or choose it from your device.
3. Pick your output settings — a smaller size or a more efficient format — and compress the image.
4. Check the result before you use it: open the compressed copy and look at it at full size, especially any text or faces.
5. Download the compressed version and upload that, keeping your original file untouched.

Because everything happens on your own device, there is no upload queue and no waiting for a server — the compressed file is ready as soon as your browser finishes processing it.

## Choose the right format

Format choice matters as much as file size:

- Photos: JPG or WebP usually give the smallest files for photographs, since they are designed for smooth colour gradients like skies and skin.
- Screenshots, logos, and graphics with text: PNG keeps sharp edges and text crisp, but the file is larger — use it when clarity matters more than size.
- Simple graphics: if the picture has few colours and large flat areas, a PNG or WebP copy can be both small and sharp.

If you are unsure, try the photo format first and compare the result with the original side by side. If text or edges look worse, switch back to the sharper format.

## Resize before you compress

Resizing is usually the biggest single saving, and it is the step people skip. Ask what size the image will actually be shown at: a profile picture, a listing photo, or a picture inside an article rarely needs to be wider than 1200–1600 pixels. Shrinking a 4000-pixel-wide phone photo down to that width can cut the file dramatically before any quality setting is even touched — and the picture looks identical on screen.

Rule of thumb: always keep the original file. Compress a copy, check the copy, and upload the copy. If a site later asks for a higher-quality version, you still have the original to work from.

## Quick checklist

- Is the image resized to roughly the size it will be displayed at?
- Is the format right for the picture — JPG or WebP for photos, PNG for sharp text and graphics?
- Have you opened the compressed copy at full size and checked text and faces?
- Is the original file safely kept, separate from the compressed copy?
- Does the compressed file now upload without hitting the site's size limit?
